title: All O`one Data Structure
description: Brute force to optimized: a plain count map with full rescans versus a doubly linked list of count buckets.

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement

Design a data structure that supports inc(key) (increment a key's count, inserting it with count 1 if new), dec(key) (decrement a key's count, removing it entirely if the count reaches 0), getMaxKey() (return any key with the current highest count), and getMinKey() (return any key with the current lowest count), with every operation running in O(1) time.

blocks.caption: A doubly linked list of count buckets keeps the current min and max always at its two ends

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Detail"],"rows":[["Input","A sequence of inc(key), dec(key), getMaxKey(), and getMinKey() calls"],["Output","getMaxKey and getMinKey return any key currently at the highest or lowest count; inc and dec update the internal state"],["Goal","Implement all four operations in O(1) time each"],["Constraints","1 <= key.length <= 10, key consists of lowercase English letters, at most 50000 calls total, at least one inc call happens before the first dec on any key"]]}

blocks.text: 2. Pattern Detection

blocks.content: {"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["Need instant access to both the current max and min count keys","Maintain an ordered structure by count, with direct pointers to both extremes"],["Counts change by exactly 1 per operation, and keys can share a count","Group keys sharing a count into \"buckets\" ordered by count value"],["Need O(1) insertion and removal of buckets anywhere in the order","A doubly linked list of buckets, with a hash map from key to its current bucket node"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem

Design a data structure that supports inc(key) (increment a key's count, inserting it with count 1 if new), dec(key) (decrement a key's count, removing it entirely if the count reaches 0), getMaxKey() (return any key with the current highest count), and getMinKey() (return any key with the current lowest count), with every operation running in O(1) time.

blocks.title: Analogy: A Leaderboard That Instantly Reports the Top and Bottom Player
blocks.text: Like a live leaderboard that needs to instantly answer "who is currently winning" and "who is currently last" after every single point scored or lost, without ever having to rescan the entire list of players to figure it out.

blocks.caption: Track every key's count so the current max and min can both be reported instantly

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
Example: inc("hello") twice, then getMaxKey and getMinKey

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["inc(\"hello\") twice","\"hello\" now has count 2, the only key present","Each inc call increases \"hello\"'s count by exactly 1, from 0 (not present) to 1, then from 1 to 2"],["getMaxKey() and getMinKey()","both return \"hello\", since it is the only key","With only one distinct key present, it is trivially both the most and least frequent simultaneously"]]}

blocks.text: Example: continuing, inc("leet"), then getMaxKey and getMinKey

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["inc(\"leet\")","\"leet\" now has count 1, \"hello\" still has count 2","Only \"leet\"'s own count is affected by its own inc call; \"hello\"'s count is untouched"],["getMaxKey()","\"hello\" (count 2, the highest)","\"hello\"'s count of 2 is strictly greater than \"leet\"'s count of 1"],["getMinKey()","\"leet\" (count 1, the lowest)","\"leet\"'s count of 1 is strictly lower than \"hello\"'s count of 2"]]}

blocks.text: Edge case: dec(key) on a key whose count reaches exactly 0
When a key's count is decremented all the way down to 0, it must be removed from the structure entirely, as if it were never inserted at all.
5. How Should We Think?

Before reaching for any structure, notice the two hardest constraints working against each other: the max and min counts change constantly as inc and dec are called, yet both must be answerable in O(1), ruling out any approach that scans to find them.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: A plain hash map from key to count answers inc and dec in O(1) easily, since updating one key's count never requires looking at any other key, but it gives no shortcut at all for finding the current max or min without scanning everything.

Observation 2: Since many different keys can share the exact same count at once, it helps to think in terms of "count buckets": one bucket per distinct count value currently in use, holding the set of keys at that count, rather than tracking each key in isolation.

Observation 3: If these buckets are kept in a doubly linked list, ordered by their count value, lowest at the front, highest at the back, then getMinKey and getMaxKey both become O(1): just read any key out of the front bucket or the back bucket.

Observation 4: A push, inc or dec, only ever moves one key from its current bucket to an immediately adjacent bucket, count plus or minus 1, so maintaining this list only ever requires inserting or removing a bucket next to the current one, an O(1) structural change, never a full re-sort.

Whenever a structure needs both "the current max" and "the current min" instantly, alongside frequent small updates, think of grouping elements by their changing value into an ordered doubly linked list of buckets, with a hash map providing O(1) access into the middle of that list.

This is the single most general version of the "bucket by a changing quantity" idea seen across this Hash Tables section: Maximum Frequency Stack only needed the max end, Top K Frequent Elements only needed a fixed-size array of buckets; this problem needs both ends live and dynamically reordered at the same time, which is exactly what a doubly linked list of buckets provides.
6. Brute Force Solution
Maintain a plain hash map from key to its current count. getMaxKey and getMinKey scan the entire hash map every time to find the key with the current highest or lowest count.
Step by step algorithm

items: Keep a hash map from key to count.
inc and dec directly update the count for a key, removing it entirely if the count reaches 0.
getMaxKey and getMinKey scan every entry in the map to find the current maximum or minimum count.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: inc safely handles both a brand new key, implicitly starting from 0, and an existing one, in a single unified update expression.
dec explicitly checks whether the new count reaches exactly 0, since the problem requires a key to be removed entirely at that point, not merely left present with a count of 0.
getMaxKey and getMinKey both guard against an empty structure first, returning an empty string immediately, since finding a max or min over an empty collection would otherwise raise an error.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force
inc and dec correctly update counts, and scanning the whole map for the true maximum or minimum count is correct, though slow.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(1) for inc and dec, but O(n) for getMaxKey and getMinKey, since both rescan the entire map.
Space: O(n), for the count map.
Limitation: the problem requires every operation, including getMaxKey and getMinKey, to run in O(1), which a full rescan can never achieve.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force's getMaxKey and getMinKey are slow for the same reason: neither one remembers anything about the relative ordering of counts between calls, so each one has to rediscover the extremes completely from scratch, even though only one key's count changed since the last call. The fix is to maintain that ordering persistently, rather than rebuilding it: keep every distinct count value currently in use as its own bucket, and keep those buckets threaded together in a doubly linked list sorted by count. Then the current minimum and maximum are always sitting literally at the two ends of that list, readable in O(1) with no search at all. The remaining work is keeping this list correctly updated as counts change: since any single inc or dec only moves one key by exactly one count step, that key only ever needs to move to an adjacent bucket in the list, an O(1) structural splice, never a re-sort of the whole ordering.

Maintain a doubly linked list of "buckets", where each bucket holds a distinct count value and the set of keys currently at that exact count. The buckets stay ordered by count along the list, though not necessarily consecutive integers, only relative order matters, with two sentinel nodes marking the very front, below the minimum, and very back, above the maximum. A separate hash map from key to the bucket node it currently belongs to gives O(1) access to any key's bucket. On inc or dec, move the key from its current bucket to the correct adjacent bucket, creating a new bucket if none exists yet at that exact count, and removing the old bucket entirely if it becomes empty. getMaxKey and getMinKey simply read the keys from the bucket just before the tail sentinel, or just after the head sentinel.
9. Optimized Solution
A doubly linked list of count buckets, with a hash map for O(1) key to bucket lookup.
Conceptual dry run for inc("hello"), inc("hello"), inc("leet")

items: inc("hello") first time: no bucket exists yet, so create a new bucket with count 1 right after the head sentinel, holding just "hello", since this is the very first key ever tracked.

inc("hello") second time: "hello" needs to move to a count-2 bucket; since no such bucket exists yet, create one right after the count-1 bucket, and remove the now-empty count-1 bucket, since "hello" was its only occupant.

inc("leet") first time: "leet" needs a count-1 bucket; the list currently only has the count-2 bucket holding "hello", so a fresh count-1 bucket is created right after the head sentinel, correctly placed before the count-2 bucket.
getMaxKey reads from the bucket just before the tail sentinel, the count-2 bucket, holding "hello", since the highest count is always whatever bucket sits closest to the tail.
getMinKey reads from the bucket just after the head sentinel, the count-1 bucket, holding "leet", since the lowest count is always whatever bucket sits closest to the head.

blocks.caption: Optimized: a doubly linked list of count buckets, min at the front, max at the back

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(1) for every operation, including getMaxKey and getMinKey.
Space: O(n), for the buckets and the key lookup maps.
Why This Works

Because the bucket list is always kept sorted by count, with sentinels marking the conceptual "below minimum" and "above maximum" ends, the bucket immediately after the head sentinel is always the true minimum count currently in use, and the bucket immediately before the tail sentinel is always the true maximum, with no need to compare anything at read time. Every inc or dec moves exactly one key to an adjacent bucket, creating it if it does not yet exist, and removing the vacated old bucket if it becomes empty, which preserves the sorted-by-count invariant automatically, since a key can only ever move to the very next or very previous count value, never skip ahead.

blocks.content: {"headers":["List position","What it represents"],"rows":[["Bucket immediately after the head sentinel","The set of keys currently at the lowest count in use"],["Bucket immediately before the tail sentinel","The set of keys currently at the highest count in use"]]}

blocks.text: Code walkthrough

items: The key-to-node map gives every currently-tracked key direct O(1) access to the specific bucket node it belongs to, something a plain doubly linked list alone could never provide.

Inserting a new bucket only ever happens immediately adjacent to an existing one, since a key's count only ever changes by exactly 1, meaning its new bucket's position relative to its old one is always fixed and known in advance.

Removing an empty bucket is checked after every move, immediately pruning any bucket that no longer holds any keys, which is what keeps the list from accumulating stale, empty buckets over many operations.

getMaxKey and getMinKey both check whether the relevant neighboring node is still the opposite sentinel before reading from it, correctly returning an empty string when the whole structure is empty rather than reading from a sentinel that holds no real keys.

blocks.text: 10. Complexity Comparison

blocks.content: {"headers":["Approach","Time","Space","Notes"],"rows":[["Brute force (plain hash map, full rescan)","O(1) for inc/dec, O(n) for getMaxKey/getMinKey","O(n)","Simple to implement, but violates the problem's O(1)-for-everything requirement"],["Optimized (doubly linked bucket list)","O(1) for every operation","O(n)","Every operation touches only a constant number of buckets and hash map entries"]]}

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

This is the definitive showcase of the "doubly linked list of buckets, keyed by a hash map" pattern for maintaining an ordered structure with O(1) operations at both ends, and the exact same pattern reappears, specialized further, in problems like LFU Cache.
Common mistakes

items: Forgetting to remove a bucket once it becomes empty, which would leave stale, keyless buckets cluttering the list and eventually returning incorrect, empty-looking results from getMaxKey or getMinKey.

Not handling the very first inc of a brand new key correctly, which needs to be treated as coming from an implicit count of 0, represented by the head sentinel, rather than assuming every key already has an existing bucket.

Checking a bucket's count value instead of its identity when deciding whether to reuse an existing adjacent bucket versus creating a new one, which can misplace a key if two unrelated buckets happen to share a coincidental property.

blocks.text: Edge cases

blocks.content: {"headers":["Edge case","Expected behavior"],"rows":[["Calling getMaxKey or getMinKey when the structure is completely empty","Returns an empty string rather than failing, since both sentinels being directly adjacent to each other signals no real buckets exist"],["A dec call that brings a key's count to exactly 0","Removes the key entirely from both hash maps, not just leaving it present with a count of 0"]]}

blocks.text: Interview tips

items: Draw the linked list of buckets explicitly as boxes with the head and tail sentinels at each end, since visualizing the structure makes the "insert after" and "remove if empty" operations far more intuitive than describing them in words alone.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Design a structure needing O(1) access to both the current max and min, with frequent updates" points toward a doubly linked list of value-grouped buckets, with sentinels at both ends and a hash map for O(1) access into the middle.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: How does this relate to LFU Cache? LFU Cache uses almost the identical frequency-bucket-linked-list structure, just combined with an additional recency ordering, typically via a small doubly linked list per frequency bucket, and a capacity eviction rule on top.

What if the structure also needed to support removing an arbitrary specific key directly, not just via dec calls? The key-to-node map already gives O(1) access to that key's bucket, so removal is a direct extension: remove it from its bucket's key set and prune the bucket if it becomes empty, exactly like an implicit dec down to 0.

Could a balanced binary search tree, ordered by count, replace the doubly linked list here? It could support similar operations, but insertion, deletion, and finding the min or max would cost O(log d) instead of O(1), where d is the number of distinct counts, which fails the problem's strict O(1) requirement.

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: The definitive, most general version of the "bucket by a changing quantity" pattern also seen in Maximum Frequency Stack, buckets with only the max end needed, and Top K Frequent Elements or Sort Characters By Frequency, a fixed-size bucket array with no dynamic reordering needed.
Directly generalizes into LFU Cache, which adds a recency dimension on top of this exact frequency-bucket structure.
Same "hash map for O(1) access into the middle of a linked list" technique as the classic LRU Cache design, just grouping by a shared count instead of giving each key its own standalone node.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(1) for inc/dec, O(n) for getMaxKey/getMinKey, O(n) space.
Optimized (doubly linked bucket list): O(1) for every operation, O(n) space.
12. Final Summary

items: Pattern: Doubly linked list of count-grouped buckets, with a hash map for O(1) access into the middle
Core Idea: Group keys sharing the same count into buckets kept in sorted order via a doubly linked list, so the true min and max are always sitting at the two ends
Time: O(1) for every operation
Space: O(n), for the buckets and the key lookup maps

Most Important Observation: When both the current max and min of a frequently-changing quantity must be instantly accessible, group by that quantity into an ordered doubly linked list of buckets rather than scanning for either extreme
Interview Difficulty: Hard
One-line memory trick: Buckets in a line, min at the front door, max at the back door
